latent_mechanisms.clinical_meaning: Carriage of S. pneumoniae, N. meningitidis, or H. influenzae in the upper airway, the most common portal of entry preceding bacteremia and meningeal seeding.
Quantitative bloodstream invasion that delivers organisms to the choroid plexus and meninges; high in pneumococcal/meningococcal disease and dominant in OPSI and Waterhouse–Friderichsen physiology.
Direct extension from otitis media, mastoiditis, sinusitis, dental/orbital infection, CSF leak, or post-neurosurgical site into the subarachnoid space.
Pathogen crossing of the BBB at choroid plexus and cerebral microvessels via host adhesin–receptor interactions (e.g., PspC–pIgR for pneumococcus, OpcA for meningococcus).

latent_mechanisms.display_name: Bacterial proliferation within the subarachnoid space
latent_mechanisms.clinical_meaning: Unrestricted multiplication in CSF due to low complement, low Ig, and poor phagocyte function; the central pathophysiologic driver of disease.

latent_mechanisms.display_name: CNS proinflammatory cytokine cascade (TNF-α, IL-1β, IL-6, MIF)
latent_mechanisms.clinical_meaning: Bacterial PAMP-triggered cytokine release from microglia, astrocytes, and recruited leukocytes; drives most of the host-mediated injury and is the target of adjunctive dexamethasone.
Massive CSF leukocyte recruitment producing the characteristic CSF profile (high WBC, neutrophil predominance, high protein, low glucose) and amplifying tissue injury via degranulation and ROS.
Cytokine- and neutrophil-mediated tight-junction disassembly and matrix metalloproteinase activity; produces vasogenic edema, contrast leakage, and high CSF protein.
Composite pathway: vasogenic edema from BBB disruption, cytotoxic edema from neuronal/astrocytic injury, and interstitial edema from impaired CSF reabsorption at arachnoid villi.
Sum of edema, hyperemia, exudate volume, and CSF outflow obstruction; mechanistic substrate for headache, vomiting, papilledema, depressed consciousness, and herniation.
Inflammation of subarachnoid arteries and veins traversing exudate; produces arterial narrowing, septic venous thrombosis, and territorial or watershed infarction.
Combined effect of raised ICP, vasculitis, vasospasm, and systemic hypotension lowering cerebral perfusion pressure and producing ischemic injury.
Hippocampal and cortical neuronal death from caspase activation, glutamate excitotoxicity, ROS, and ischemia; substrate for cognitive sequelae and seizures.
Spread of pus through the cochlear aqueduct producing inner ear inflammation, hair-cell loss, and sensorineural hearing loss; especially common in pneumococcal and Hib disease.
Obstruction of CSF flow at arachnoid villi (communicating) or aqueduct/foramina (obstructive) by purulent exudate, with risk of acute decompensation.
Cortical irritation from inflammation, infarction, hyponatremia, and metabolic derangements producing focal or generalized seizures and status epilepticus.
Cytokine and pain-mediated nonosmotic ADH release producing euvolemic hyponatremia that worsens cerebral edema and seizure risk.
Endotoxin/PAMP-driven systemic vasoplegia, capillary leak, and cardiac depression producing hypotension, lactic acidosis, and multiorgan dysfunction.
Tissue factor-driven systemic coagulation activation with consumptive coagulopathy and microthrombosis; particularly fulminant in meningococcal disease.
Bilateral adrenal hemorrhagic infarction in fulminant meningococcemia (and rarely pneumococcal OPSI), producing acute primary adrenal insufficiency.

mechanism_edges.clinical_rationale: Mucosal breach by colonizing organisms (pneumococcus, meningococcus, Hib) seeds the bloodstream, especially after antecedent viral URI.
Direct extension from sinusitis/otitis/mastoiditis/CSF-leak/postoperative wound delivers organisms into subarachnoid space without obligate bacteremia.
Sustained high-grade bacteremia is required for BBB transcytosis at choroid plexus and cerebral microvessels.
Once organisms enter the immunoprivileged subarachnoid space, low complement and low Ig allow rapid log-fold proliferation.
Bacterial PAMPs (LTA, peptidoglycan, LPS, pneumolysin) activate TLR2/4 on microglia and astrocytes triggering TNF-α/IL-1β/IL-6 release.
IL-8/CXCL family chemokines drive massive neutrophil chemotaxis across post-capillary venules into CSF.
Cytokines and MMP-9 disassemble tight junctions and degrade basal lamina, producing vasogenic permeability.
Neutrophil ROS and proteases amplify endothelial injury beyond cytokine effects.
Vasogenic component of edema is a direct consequence of barrier failure with plasma protein efflux.
Purulent exudate obstructs arachnoid CSF reabsorption (interstitial edema) and contributes to cytotoxic edema via neuronal injury.
Increased brain water within a fixed-volume cranial vault elevates ICP per the Monro–Kellie doctrine.
Obstruction of CSF circulation by purulent exudate raises ICP independent of parenchymal edema.
Pus blocks arachnoid villi and basal cisterns, the structural cause of communicating hydrocephalus.
Subarachnoid arteries traversing exudate develop neutrophilic phlebitis/arteritis with intimal thickening and vasospasm.
Vasculitic narrowing and septic venous thrombosis directly produce territorial and venous infarcts.
CPP = MAP – ICP; rising ICP at fixed MAP reduces cerebral perfusion to ischemic thresholds.
Ischemia drives glutamate excitotoxicity and necrosis; combined with cytokine-mediated apoptosis produces hippocampal neuronal loss.
TNF-α and reactive oxygen/nitrogen species drive caspase-mediated neuronal apoptosis independent of ischemia.
Pus migrates through the cochlear aqueduct and modiolus producing suppurative labyrinthitis and hair cell loss.
Cytokines and pain stimulate nonosmotic ADH release; SIADH occurs in roughly 30–50% of cases.
Cortical injury and gliosis create epileptogenic foci responsible for acute and remote symptomatic seizures.
Cortical infarcts are a leading driver of focal-onset and secondarily generalized seizures.
Hyponatremia lowers seizure threshold and worsens cerebral edema.
Endotoxin (meningococcal LOS) and pneumolysin drive systemic vasoplegia and capillary leak.
Endothelial activation and tissue factor exposure trigger consumptive coagulopathy.
Adrenal microthrombosis and hemorrhagic infarction cause acute primary adrenal insufficiency in fulminant meningococcemia.
Systemic hypotension reduces MAP and therefore CPP, compounding ICP-driven hypoperfusion.
Gram stain becomes positive once CSF organism load exceeds ~10^5 CFU/mL.
Direct microbiologic confirmation of CSF bacterial proliferation prior to antibiotic exposure.
Anaerobic glycolysis by bacteria and leukocytes raises CSF lactate, often >4 mmol/L in bacterial meningitis.
Bacterial and leukocyte glycolysis consume CSF glucose producing hypoglycorrhachia (CSF/serum ratio <0.4).
Massive neutrophil influx; typical CSF WBC 1,000–10,000/µL in untreated bacterial meningitis.
Neutrophil predominance (>80%) is the canonical CSF differential in pyogenic meningitis.
Plasma protein leak across disrupted BBB elevates CSF protein, often >100 mg/dL.
Direct manometric reflection of raised ICP; opening pressure typically >20 cmH2O and may exceed 40 cmH2O.
IL-1/IL-6/TNF-α act on hypothalamic OVLT to elevate set point; fever is present in ~95%.
Inflammation of meninges produces reflex paraspinal muscle spasm on neck flexion.
Lumbosacral nerve root irritation by inflamed meninges produces resistance to leg extension at hip flexion.
Reflex hip and knee flexion on neck flexion from cervical meningeal traction.
Horizontal head rotation worsens headache from inflamed meninges; sensitive but not specific.
Stretch of dura and pain-sensitive vessels by raised ICP.
Optic disc swelling from impaired axoplasmic flow at the lamina cribrosa; less common in fulminant cases due to short time course.
Reduced CPP and thalamocortical dysfunction produce drowsiness, confusion, and coma.
Cytokine-induced encephalopathy contributes to altered consciousness independent of ICP.
Inflammation envelops cranial nerves at the skull base, classically affecting CN III, VI, VII, and VIII.
Raised ICP causes false-localizing CN VI palsy; uncal herniation produces CN III palsy.
Sensorineural hearing loss develops in ~10–30% of bacterial meningitis survivors and is the most common neurologic sequel.
Direct clinical manifestation of cortical hyperexcitability; seizures occur in 15–30% of cases.
Territorial or watershed infarction produces focal motor, sensory, or language deficits.
Direct radiographic correlate visible on CT/MRI as effaced sulci, compressed ventricles, and loss of gray–white differentiation.
Ventricular dilation visible on imaging; communicating type predominates.
DWI/MRI demonstrates arterial and venous territorial infarcts in 15–25% of severe cases.
Inflamed meninges enhance with gadolinium on MRI and reflect active disease extent.
Blood cultures positive in 50–80% of pneumococcal/Hib meningitis and 50–60% of meningococcal disease before antibiotics.
Microvascular thrombosis and vasculitis produce nonblanching petechiae and purpura, characteristically meningococcal.
Confluent retiform purpura with skin necrosis from extensive dermal microthrombosis; herald of fulminant meningococcemia.
Consumption thrombocytopenia is a defining feature of DIC.
Consumption coagulopathy reduces fibrinogen.
Fibrin breakdown products markedly elevated in DIC.
Vasoplegia and capillary leak reduce MAP; vasopressor requirement defines septic shock.
Tissue hypoperfusion drives anaerobic glycolysis; lactate >2 mmol/L is a sepsis marker.
Compensatory tachycardia from hypotension and fever.
Compensatory tachypnea for metabolic acidosis and cytokine effects on respiratory centers.
Marrow demargination and release of band forms; OPSI and severe sepsis can paradoxically produce leukopenia.
IL-6-driven hepatic acute phase response; CRP usually >100 mg/L.
Procalcitonin rises sharply in bacterial bloodstream infection and helps distinguish from viral meningitis.
Free water retention produces euvolemic hyponatremia.
Bilateral adrenal hemorrhagic necrosis causes refractory shock unresponsive to catecholamines without steroid replacement.
Sustained ICP elevation precipitates uncal, central, or tonsillar herniation.
Refractory or repeated seizures convert to status, particularly with cortical infarction or hyponatremia.
Acute hydrocephalus may require external ventricular drainage to prevent herniation.
Permanent hearing loss in 10–30% overall, up to 30% with pneumococcal disease.
Vasculitic occlusion of perforator and cortical arteries produces clinically significant stroke.
Vessel wall injury combined with DIC and venous thrombosis can produce hemorrhagic conversion.
Direct event manifestation; septic shock complicates 10–30% of bacterial meningitis cases.
Direct hazard correlate.
Septic AKI from hypoperfusion, microthrombosis, and inflammatory tubular injury.
Sepsis-associated ARDS may develop, particularly after fluid resuscitation.
Depressed consciousness, airway protection, and ICP control drive intubation.
Refractory ICP with herniation is the dominant mode of CNS death.
Refractory shock with multiorgan failure is the dominant mode of systemic death, especially in meningococcal sepsis.
Without immediate stress-dose steroids and antibiotics, mortality of fulminant meningococcemia exceeds 40%.

Tachycardia from fever and sepsis; bradycardia with raised ICP (Cushing reflex) is an ominous late sign.
Maintained early; falls in septic shock; rises with Cushing reflex in late herniation.
Hypotension <90 mmHg defines hemodynamic instability.
Tachypnea early; abnormal patterns (Cheyne–Stokes, ataxic) with brainstem compromise.
Usually preserved unless ARDS, aspiration pneumonia, or respiratory depression from raised ICP.
Falls progressively with cytokine encephalopathy and rising ICP; GCS ≤8 is a key prognostic threshold.
Markedly elevated in untreated bacterial meningitis; values >40 cmH2O carry herniation risk.
Typically 1,000–10,000/μL in untreated disease; profoundly low counts despite high pathogen load suggest severe immunosuppression.
Neutrophil predominance >0.8; lymphocytic shift may occur after several days of antibiotic treatment or in early Listeria.
Elevated, typically >100 mg/dL, reflecting BBB disruption.
Low; CSF/serum ratio <0.4 supports bacterial etiology.
Ratio <0.4 strongly supports bacterial meningitis; <0.23 highly specific.
Useful particularly in postoperative meningitis where other CSF parameters are confounded; values >3.5–4 mmol/L favor bacterial etiology.
Positive in 60–90% pretreatment; sensitivity falls 20–30% after even a single antibiotic dose.
Positive in 70–85% pretreatment; sterilization can occur within 2–4 hours of effective antibiotics for meningococcus.
Multiplex PCR (e.g., FilmArray) sensitivity >90% even after antibiotics; useful for diagnosis when cultures are negative.
Latex agglutination for pneumococcus, meningococcus, Hib, GBS; supplemental when stains/cultures are negative.

Bandemia >10% supports severe bacterial infection.
Falls with DIC; thrombocytopenia <100 is an ICU-severity marker.
Usually preserved early; falls with hemorrhagic complications.
Markedly elevated, usually >100 mg/L; supports bacterial over viral etiology.
Highly discriminating between bacterial (>0.5–2 ng/mL) and viral meningitis.
Elevated in shock; >2 mmol/L marks tissue hypoperfusion, >4 mmol/L marks severe sepsis.
Rises with septic AKI.
Falls with SIADH; hyponatremia <130 worsens cerebral edema.
Stress hyperglycemia common; drives the CSF/serum glucose ratio interpretation.
Falls in DIC; baseline elevation as acute phase reactant may mask early consumption.
Markedly elevated in DIC.
Prolonged in DIC and septic hepatic dysfunction.
Prolonged with consumption coagulopathy.
Positive in 50–80% of pneumococcal/Hib, 50–60% of meningococcal disease, before antibiotics.
Quantitatively high in fulminant meningococcal disease; correlates with mortality.
Cumulative organ dysfunction; rising SOFA reflects worsening sepsis.
Categorical pathogen identification: pneumococcus / meningococcus / Listeria / Hib / Group B Strep / E. coli / S. aureus / other gram-negative; drives empiric and definitive therapy.
MIC drives whether penicillin/ceftriaxone monotherapy is sufficient; meningitis breakpoints are stricter than for pneumonia.
Probability that the responsible organism is ceftriaxone-susceptible at meningitis breakpoints; determines need for adjunctive vancomycin.
Local prevalence of penicillin- and cephalosporin-resistant pneumococci; determines empiric vancomycin and rifampin selection.
Fever present in ~95%; absence raises suspicion of immunocompromise or atypical pathogens.
Severe holocephalic headache, present in ~85%, often the earliest symptom.
Resistance to passive neck flexion; present in ~70% of adults but often absent in elderly and immunocompromised.
Specific but insensitive (~5–10% sensitivity) for bacterial meningitis.
Specific but insensitive; absence does not exclude meningitis.
Worsening of headache with horizontal head rotation; sensitive but not specific in early studies.
Light intolerance from meningeal irritation.
Confusion, drowsiness, or coma; present in ~70% on presentation.
Focal or generalized seizures in 15–30%; more common with pneumococcal disease and cortical infarction.
Late marker of raised ICP; absence does not exclude elevated ICP in fulminant disease.
Most often CN VI (false-localizing), III (uncal herniation), VII, or VIII.
Hemiparesis, aphasia, or ataxia from cerebritis, infarction, or vasculitis; in 10–30% of cases.
Nonblanching petechiae/purpura, classically meningococcal; presence requires immediate empiric antibiotics.
Confluent retiform purpura with skin necrosis; herald of fulminant meningococcemia and DIC.
Often projectile, from raised ICP and meningeal irritation.
Sensorineural hearing loss in 10–30% of survivors; assess with audiometry before discharge.
Hypertension with bradycardia and irregular respiration; late, ominous sign of impending herniation.
Unilateral pupillary dilatation suggests uncal herniation with CN III compression.
Effaced sulci, compressed ventricles, loss of gray–white differentiation on CT/MRI.
Ventricular dilation; communicating type predominates in pneumococcal disease.
DWI-positive territorial or watershed infarcts in 15–25% of severe cases.
Diffuse pial-arachnoid enhancement on post-gadolinium MRI; basal predominance suggests TB but is also seen in pneumococcal disease.
Ependymal enhancement and intraventricular debris on MRI; common with pneumococcal and gram-negative meningitis and ventriculostomy-associated disease.
Particularly with sinusitis or otitis media as source; surgical drainage frequently required.
Ring-enhancing parenchymal lesion; uncommon coexistence but changes therapy and demands neurosurgical evaluation.
Opacified mastoid air cells indicate contiguous source requiring ENT involvement.
Sphenoid or ethmoid sinusitis is a particularly dangerous parameningeal source.
Acute otitis media as portal of pneumococcal/Hib meningitis, especially in children.
Cribriform plate or temporal bone defect on high-resolution CT; underlies recurrent pneumococcal meningitis.
Cortical or sinus thrombosis on MRV; produces venous infarcts and refractory ICP.
Hours-scale variable; door-to-antibiotic time of <1h and door-to-LP-or-empiric-treatment of <60 min materially improve outcome.
CSF AUC/MIC adequacy. Reduced for 1st-gen cephs, aminoglycosides, and some vancomycin doses; enhanced by inflamed meninges and dexamethasone reduces vancomycin penetration.

Vancomycin (± rifampin) added empirically until susceptibilities return when local DRSP rates are appreciable.
Dexamethasone must be given just before or with the first antibiotic dose; benefit is lost if started after antibiotics in adults.
Surgical or functional asplenia raises risk and severity of pneumococcal/Hib/meningococcal disease.
C5–C9 or properdin deficiency, or eculizumab/ravulizumab use, dramatically raises meningococcal risk.
Prior or current CSF leak, often pneumococcal recurrent meningitis.
Recent craniotomy, EVD, or shunt placement broadens empiric coverage to include staphylococci and gram-negatives including Pseudomonas.
Markedly increases pneumococcal meningitis risk.
PCV13/PCV15/PCV20 and PPSV23 status; reduces invasive pneumococcal disease.
MenACWY ± MenB; reduces invasive meningococcal disease especially in adolescents and complement-deficient patients.
Hib conjugate vaccine has nearly eliminated Hib meningitis in vaccinated populations.
Excludes beta-lactams (use moxifloxacin + vancomycin + TMP-SMX for Listeria) only when truly type 1.
HIV, transplant, biologics, high-dose steroids; broadens differential to include Listeria, Cryptococcus, TB.
Neonate, infant, child, adult, elderly: drives empiric regimen and pathogen spectrum.
Drainage of mastoid, sinus, subdural empyema, brain abscess, or removal of infected hardware required for cure.
Whether identified surgical source has been adequately drained or removed.
Rifampin/ciprofloxacin/ceftriaxone for close contacts of confirmed meningococcal disease within 24h ideal.
Risk peaks days 1–4 with maximal edema; LP without prior imaging in patients with focal deficit/altered consciousness can precipitate herniation.

Particularly with ventriculostomy and gram-negative organisms.
Vasculitis-related stroke complicates ~15–25% of severe pneumococcal cases.
Less common but devastating; arises from DIC, septic venous thrombosis, or hemorrhagic conversion of infarcts.

From shock and aminoglycoside/vancomycin nephrotoxicity.

Overall in-hospital mortality 10–30%; pneumococcal 20–37%, meningococcal 5–15% in resourced settings, OPSI/Waterhouse–Friderichsen >40%, Listeria 15–30%, Hib <5% with treatment.

axis_couplings.clinical_rationale: Ratio is derived from CSF glucose normalized to serum glucose; correlated by construction but ratio is more discriminating.
Bacterial and leukocyte glycolysis concurrently consume glucose and produce lactate.
Both are driven by neutrophilic chemotaxis; lymphocytic shift after antibiotics dissociates them.
Both rise with bacterial inflammation but kinetics differ; PCT rises faster and falls faster.
Both fall together in DIC consumption.
Falling MAP drives tissue hypoperfusion and rising lactate.
GCS quantifies the same construct; near-redundant but on different scales.
Petechiae can rapidly coalesce into purpura fulminans in fulminant meningococcemia.
Septic shock precedes and mechanistically drives DIC.
DIC microthrombosis triggers Waterhouse–Friderichsen adrenal hemorrhage.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Pneumococcus, meningococcus, Hib, and most enteric gram-negatives are susceptible at meningitis breakpoints.
DRSP with cefotaxime MIC ≥1 µg/mL requires adjunctive vancomycin.
True type 1 hypersensitivity demands non-beta-lactam regimen.
Add ampicillin in patients >50 or immunocompromised for Listeria coverage.

treatments.context_specific_role: Backbone of empiric and most definitive regimens for community-acquired bacterial meningitis in patients without true beta-lactam allergy.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Preferred in neonates over ceftriaxone (which displaces bilirubin and precipitates with calcium).
DRSP requires adjunctive vancomycin.

treatments.context_specific_role: Substitutable alternative to ceftriaxone, preferred in neonates.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Empirically added for DRSP coverage until pneumococcal susceptibilities return.
MRSA and coagulase-negative staphylococci in postoperative meningitis.
Dexamethasone reduces meningeal inflammation and CSF vancomycin penetration; consider adjunctive rifampin or higher trough targets.

side_effects.interpretation: Trough/AUC-related nephrotoxicity, especially with concurrent piperacillin-tazobactam or aminoglycosides.

treatments.context_specific_role: Empiric DRSP coverage and definitive MRSA coverage in postoperative meningitis.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Patients >50 require Listeria coverage that cephalosporins cannot provide.
Cell-mediated immunity defect predisposes to Listeria.
Pregnancy raises Listeria risk.

treatments.context_specific_role: Listeria coverage in age >50, immunocompromised, pregnant; also Group B Strep and enterococci in neonates.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Listeria coverage in true beta-lactam–allergic patients.

side_effects.interpretation: Hyperkalemia from collecting duct ENaC blockade.
Pseudo-rise from tubular secretion blockade and true AKI.

treatments.context_specific_role: Substitute for ampicillin in beta-lactam–allergic patients needing Listeria coverage.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Broad gram-negative coverage including ESBL, plus Listeria activity.
Active against many resistant pneumococci.

side_effects.interpretation: Lower seizure risk than imipenem but not zero.

treatments.context_specific_role: Postoperative/healthcare-associated meningitis, severe penicillin allergy without anaphylaxis history, multidrug-resistant organisms.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Pseudomonas coverage in postoperative meningitis.

side_effects.interpretation: Cefepime neurotoxicity in renal impairment can mimic worsening encephalopathy.

treatments.context_specific_role: Substitute for ceftriaxone when Pseudomonas coverage needed (postoperative, neutropenic).

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Backbone option for severe beta-lactam allergy in suspected pneumococcal/meningococcal disease.

treatments.context_specific_role: Beta-lactam–allergic patients in combination with vancomycin and TMP-SMX for full coverage.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Adjunct for highly cephalosporin-resistant pneumococcus when vancomycin penetration is reduced by dexamethasone.
Compensates for reduced vancomycin CSF penetration.

treatments.context_specific_role: Adjunct in DRSP, also chemoprophylaxis option for meningococcal close contacts.

Possible harm in low-resource settings with HIV-TB coinfection

treatments.context_specific_role: Acute ICP control while definitive measures (CSF diversion, decompression) are arranged.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: First-line vasopressor in septic shock to maintain MAP ≥65 mmHg.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Catecholamine-resistant septic shock and presumed Waterhouse–Friderichsen require stress-dose hydrocortisone.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Drainage essential for cure.
Mastoidectomy when complicated by intracranial extension.
Definitive CSF leak repair prevents recurrent meningitis.

treatments.context_specific_role: Drainage of subdural empyema, mastoidectomy, sinus drainage, abscess evacuation, CSF leak repair, infected hardware removal.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Eliminates nasopharyngeal carriage in close contacts of confirmed meningococcal disease.

treatments.context_specific_role: Public health intervention for close contacts of meningococcal cases, alternatives include single-dose ciprofloxacin or ceftriaxone.

neonate.trajectory_modulation: Group B Strep, E. coli, Listeria predominate; nuchal rigidity often absent; bulging fontanelle and lethargy are key signs.

infant_young_child.trajectory_modulation: Pneumococcus, meningococcus, Hib (if unvaccinated); seizures more common.

young_adult.trajectory_modulation: Meningococcus disproportionately represented in dormitory and military populations.

elderly.trajectory_modulation: Listeria emerges, atypical presentations without fever or meningismus, higher mortality.

present.trajectory_modulation: Encapsulated organisms (pneumococcus, meningococcus, Hib) with risk of OPSI; mortality up to 50% without rapid antibiotics.
Recurrent meningococcal disease across serogroups including non-vaccine strains; demands MenACWY+MenB vaccination and prophylactic antibiotics.
Recurrent pneumococcal meningitis; high-resolution CT to identify cribriform/temporal bone defect; surgical repair prevents recurrence.
Staphylococci (including MRSA), gram-negative bacilli (including Pseudomonas), and Cutibacterium predominate; expand empiric coverage to vancomycin + cefepime/meropenem.
Pneumococcal meningitis risk markedly increased; pneumococcal vaccination essential.

otitis_media_mastoiditis.trajectory_modulation: Pneumococcus, S. aureus, anaerobes via direct extension.

sinusitis.trajectory_modulation: Sphenoid/ethmoid sinusitis particularly dangerous; mixed flora and S. milleri group.

endocarditis_or_pneumonia.trajectory_modulation: Hematogenous seeding from pneumococcal pneumonia (Austrian syndrome) or staphylococcal endocarditis.

hiv_advanced.trajectory_modulation: Cryptococcus, TB, atypical pathogens; pyogenic meningitis still occurs.

transplant_or_biologic.trajectory_modulation: Listeria especially with TNF inhibitors and rituximab; atypical pathogens.

present.trajectory_modulation: Pneumococcus, Listeria; impaired phagocytosis and complement.
Pneumococcal and gram-negative meningitis modestly increased; worse outcomes.
Listeria monocytogenes risk markedly elevated due to T-cell tolerance; ampicillin essential in empiric coverage.

dormitory_or_military_or_pilgrimage.trajectory_modulation: Meningococcal outbreaks; vaccination and chemoprophylaxis are public health priorities.

sub_saharan_africa_dry_season.trajectory_modulation: Meningococcal serogroups A, C, W, X epidemics.

fully_vaccinated_pcv_menacwy_hib.trajectory_modulation: Substantial protection against vaccine-covered serotypes/serogroups; non-vaccine strains can still cause disease.

unvaccinated.trajectory_modulation: Hib disease re-emerges; broader pneumococcal serotype range.

supportive_care: ICU admission for hourly neuro checks and continuous hemodynamic monitoring in any patient with altered consciousness, focal deficit, seizure, hemodynamic instability, or fulminant rash.
Door-to-antibiotic time target <60 minutes from presentation; do not delay empiric antibiotics for CT or LP when meningitis is suspected.
Pre-LP CT head only when focal deficit, new seizure, immunocompromised state, GCS ≤10, or papilledema is present; otherwise do LP first.
Adjunctive dexamethasone 0.15 mg/kg q6h × 4 days given just before or with the first antibiotic dose in suspected pneumococcal disease in adults and Hib in children.
Head of bed elevation 30°, midline neutral neck, normocapnia (PaCO2 35–40 mmHg), normothermia, and normoglycemia for ICP control.
Sodium and fluid management: euvolemia, treat hyponatremia carefully, avoid free water; hypertonic saline or mannitol for refractory ICP.
Continuous EEG monitoring in obtunded patients to detect non-convulsive seizures; levetiracetam for clinical or electrographic seizures.
Serial neuroimaging (MRI preferred) for clinical deterioration, focal deficit, persistent fever after 72h, or to assess hydrocephalus, infarct, empyema, or abscess.
Repeat LP at 48–72h in gram-negative or DRSP meningitis to confirm CSF sterilization.
Audiology evaluation before discharge in all survivors and structured neurorehabilitation referral for cognitive, motor, and seizure sequelae.
Public health notification for meningococcal and Hib disease; rifampin/ciprofloxacin/ceftriaxone chemoprophylaxis for close contacts within 24h of diagnosis.
Vaccination of survivors and at-risk household members against pneumococcus, meningococcus, and Hib; evaluate for asplenia and complement deficiency in unusual or recurrent disease.
Stress-ulcer prophylaxis, mechanical DVT prophylaxis (pharmacologic when DIC has resolved), and early enteral nutrition.
Source control: ENT/neurosurgery consultation for mastoidectomy, sinus drainage, subdural empyema or brain abscess evacuation, infected hardware removal, and CSF leak repair.
Family communication and goals-of-care discussion for patients with extensive cerebral infarction, refractory ICP, or persistent vegetative state.
